extracted.intended_audience: readers and students of political philosophy, theology, and church–state relations
extracted.subtask_description: Extracts and summarizes normative claims about ecclesiastical authority, pastoral functions, and church revenue as presented in a political-theological treatise (chapter-level excerpt). Focuses on who may ordain, maintain, and discipline clergy and how religious power relates to civil sovereignty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Signs of true believers
rubrics_metrics.description: “These signs follow them that beleeve in my Name; they shall cast out Devills; they shall speak with new tongues; They shall take up Serpents, and if they drink any deadly thing, it shall not hurt them; They shall lay hands on the sick, and they shall recover.” (S. Marke chap.16.17.)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used to identify 'true Beleevers' in the text: the author argues that such signs accompanied apostolic ministry and that Philip could not confer what the apostles did; implication is that baptism by an apostle conferred extraordinary power, whereas ordinary ministers may not confer such signs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Selection of deacons by the congregation
rubrics_metrics.description: The first Deacons were chosen, not by the Apostles, but by a Congregation of the Disciples (Acts 6): the Twelve told the disciples to 'looke you out among you seven men... whom we may appoint over this businesse', and 'the saying pleased the multitude, and they chose seven'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Process-standard: the congregation selects; apostles/public authorities declare or confirm. Historical precedent (Acts 6) is used as normative evidence for congregational choice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Qualifications for deacons (qualities required)
rubrics_metrics.description: Men chosen should be 'of honest report, full of the Holy Ghost, and of Wisdome' (Acts 6:3).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Specifies substantive personal qualifications for ecclesiastical officeholders: reputation, spiritual character, and wisdom. The text treats these as criteria the congregation should apply when choosing officers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ecclesiastical revenue under Mosaic law (tithes and priestly portions)
rubrics_metrics.description: Under the Old Testament, the Tribe of Levi were assigned certain cities and 'the tenth of the fruits of the land' for their portion; Priests had 'the tenth of that tenth, together with part of the oblations, and sacrifices.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains the historical/legal source of priestly maintenance under a theocratic civil order and ties the right of tythes to the civil/political status of God as king in Israel (i.e., constituted by civil power).

rubrics_metrics.name: Right of tithes constituted by civil power
rubrics_metrics.description: Because God was then King and Moses/Aaron were his lieutenants, 'the Right of Tythes, and Offerings was constituted by the Civill Power.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Normative claim: the entitlement to public ecclesiastical revenue derives from the civil polity in which a public person (the king) dispenses public revenues; tithes are therefore a civil institution in origin.

rubrics_metrics.name: Church livings determined by the civil sovereign
rubrics_metrics.description: After changes (e.g., return from Captivity), 'Church Livings were determined by the Civill Soveraign.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Historical/legal claim used normatively: maintenance and legal status of church offices depend on the civil sovereign's authority and laws, not solely on ecclesiastical custom.

rubrics_metrics.name: Early Christian ministers maintained by voluntary contribution
rubrics_metrics.description: In our Saviour's time and after, Christians of every city lived in common 'upon the mony which was made of the sale of their lands and possessions' and ministers' maintenance 'was nothing but the voluntary contribution of them that had embraced their Doctrine.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Norm: before imperial establishment (Constantine), ministerial support was voluntary benevolence rather than compulsory tithing; examples include women who ministered of their substance and the communal sale of goods (Acts 4:34).

rubrics_metrics.name: Ministers should 'live of the Gospel' but not determine their own allowance
rubrics_metrics.description: Paul: 'Even so hath the Lord appointed, that they which preach the Gospel should live of the Gospel.' But their allowance 'must needs therefore be determined, either by the gratitude, and liberality of every particular man of their flock, or by the whole Congregation.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguishes principle (ministers deserve maintenance) from mechanism (they should not self-determine compensation). Where civil law lacked enforcement, maintenance was by voluntary giving or congregational determination.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sovereign's right to judge doctrines fit for peace
rubrics_metrics.description: The Right of Judging what Doctrines are fit for Peace, and to be taught the Subjects, is in all Common-wealths inseparably annexed to the Soveraign Power Civill.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Political principle: control over public teaching (including religion) is a sovereign function because opinions influence actions and public order; thus doctrinal regulation is justified by preservation of the commonwealth.

rubrics_metrics.name: Christian kings as Supreme Pastors with power to ordain
rubrics_metrics.description: Christian Kings are still the Supreme Pastors of their people, and have power to ordain what Pastors they please, to teach the Church, that is, to teach the People committed to their charge.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Normative claim that converts pre-existing sovereign pastoral powers into the Christian context: kings may appoint teachers, set titles, and make laws for maintenance (tithes or otherwise) provided they act from sincere conscience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pastoral authority: jure civili vs jure divino
rubrics_metrics.description: All Pastors, except the Supreme, execute their charges by the Authority of the Civill Soveraign (Jure Civili). But the King and every other Soveraign executeth his Office of Supreme Pastor by immediate Authority from God (Jure Divino).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Conceptual distinction: ordinary clerical authority is delegated civil authority; the sovereign's pastoral authority is treated as derivative from God. The text draws practical consequences (e.g., titulature 'Dei Gratia Rex').

rubrics_metrics.name: Sovereigns may perform pastoral sacraments and consecrations
rubrics_metrics.description: If every Christian Soveraign be the Supreme Pastor, it seemeth that he hath also the Authority... to Baptize, and to Administer the Sacrament of the Lords Supper; and to Consecrate both Temples, and Pastors to Gods service.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Affirms theoretical competence of sovereigns to do sacramental/pastoral acts but notes practical reasons (burden of government) why they usually delegate; analogies (kings could lecture or sit in judgment) and scriptural examples (Christ and Paul baptized few because of larger charge).

rubrics_metrics.name: Imposition of hands as designation ceremony
rubrics_metrics.description: Imposition of Hands... was a most ancient publique ceremony... designed and made certain the person intended in a mans prayer, blessing, sacrifice, consecration... The Apostles, and Presbyters, and the Presbytery it self, Laid Hands on them whom they ordained Pastors, and withall prayed for them that they might receive the Holy Ghost.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Functional rule: laying on of hands serves to designate and publicly mark ordination. But the text argues it is a designatory rite rather than the source of authority when civil sovereignty already confers right.

rubrics_metrics.name: Imposition unnecessary when civil sovereignty grants authority
rubrics_metrics.description: If there had been then any Christian, that had had the Power of Teaching before; the Baptizing of him... had given him no new Power... and therefore the Imposition of Hands had been unnecessary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Argument: when the sovereign already possesses the right to ordain/teach, the ordinary ceremonial imposition of hands is not strictly necessary to confer authority; sovereignty can authorize without the rite.

rubrics_metrics.name: Delegation of religious government is civil and revocable
rubrics_metrics.description: If they please... they may commit the government of their Subjects in matters of Religion to the Pope; but then the Pope is in that point Subordinate to them, and exerciseth that Charge in anothers Dominion Jure Civili, ... and may therefore be discharged of that Office, when the Soveraign for the good of his Subjects shall think it necessary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Norm: any transfer of ecclesiastical governance to a foreign authority is delegation under civil law and can be revoked by the sovereign; foreign ecclesiastical authority in a realm is not independent jure divino within that realm.

rubrics_metrics.name: Civil enforcement required for effective ecclesiastical censures
rubrics_metrics.description: It is he that giveth strength to Excommunications; which but for such Laws and Punishments, as may humble obstinate Libertines, and reduce them to union with the rest of the Church, would bee contemned.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical point: ecclesiastical censures (e.g., excommunication) rely on civil punishments and laws to have force in the commonwealth; without civil backing, ecclesiastical penalties are ineffective.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interpretation of 'Thou art Peter' — foundation is confession, not person
rubrics_metrics.description: The place 'Thou art Peter, And upon this rock I will build my Church'... proveth no more, but that the Church of Christ hath for foundation one onely Article... Peter answered (for them all) 'Thou art Christ, the Son of the Living God;' which... is the Foundation of the Faith of the whole Church.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hermeneutic standard: the 'rock' is interpreted as the fundamental article of faith (confession of Christ) rather than as establishing a perpetual personal monarchy in Peter; used to argue against universal papal monarchy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Essential marks of Antichrist
rubrics_metrics.description: Antichrist in the proper signification hath two essentiall marks; One, that he denyeth Jesus to be the Christ; and another that he professeth himselfe to bee Christ.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Defines criteria for labeling a figure 'Antichrist': either denial of Christ's incarnation or self-assertion as Christ. The text applies this definition to argue that the Pope, who neither denies nor claims to be Christ, does not meet the proper signification of Antichrist.
